title: Peekaboo! The story of Canada’s moving island
description:
A floating island that appeared in a Canadian reservoir and seemed to vanish has returned. Officials at Williston Reservoir in British Columbia spent months tracking it through satellite imagery and discovered it had drifted 30 kilometres away. The island made international headlines and gained a loyal fan base on social media. Jake Horton from BBC Verify has been looking at the data and gave us an overview of what we can confirm about the island’s story. Plus, Jon Dickson, who specialising in marine wood and sea restoration tells us all about floating islands, and what it’s like to be on one.

Email: whatintheworld@bbc.co.uk WhatsApp: +44 330 12 33 22 6 Presenter: Hannah Gelbart Producers: Mollie Perella and Benita Barden Editor: Verity Wilde
summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討加拿大不列顛哥倫比亞省 Williston 水庫一座會移動的漂浮島嶼及其背後的科學原理。BBC Verify 記者 Jake Horton 利用衛星資料證實，這座長滿 300 至 400 棵樹木、面積相當於 2 個足球場大的島嶼，在幾週內漂移了超過 30 公里。專家 Jon Dickson 解釋，此類漂浮島嶼是由厚實苔蘚層與淺根樹木組成，樹冠如同船帆般受風力推動而在水面上移動。專家也提醒民眾切勿登島以維護安全，並指出漂浮植被在海洋中能充當「浮動自助餐」，為魚類等海洋生物提供重要的棲地與食物來源。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores the mystery of a floating, moving island in British Columbia's Williston Reservoir in Canada. BBC Verify's Jake Horton explains how satellite imagery confirmed local reports that the island—covered in 300 to 400 trees and roughly the size of two football pitches—drifted over 30 kilometers in just a few weeks. Expert Jon Dickson describes how these floating islands form from thick moss layers and shallow-rooted trees, drifting when wind pushes the tree canopy like a sail. He warns against walking on the unstable formation and highlights how floating islands serve as vital ecosystems and floating food sources for marine life in open waters.
